- Proclus on the world soul in the psychogony, In Tim. II.
- The Pyramid Texts themselves are not held; Pepi's star-ba is known through Budge.

title: 5. Where souls come from
md:
**The question.** If a person has a soul, where did it come from? It might have existed before the body,
come down from a higher world, been passed on by the parents with the body, been made new by God for each
body, or begun with the body. Or the question may have no answer, because the soul was never made at all.
The answer decides much else: whether we can remember a former life, whether sin is inherited, whether
souls differ by people, and whether anything could be given a soul.

**How to read it.** ✓ claims are verified on a Source Library page; ◐ are hedged. Quotes are SL's English
(a model translation of the page) unless the book is in English or the original is given. Claims in sibling
KBs are written `aliveness-kb:<id>` or `nous-kb:<id>`. All claims here carry `q:origin`.
Plural-soul systems are on [09-many-souls.md](/explore/histories/soul/09-many-souls).

**The short answer.**
- **It existed before the body**, and learning is remembering: the Phaedo, Glanvill, the Kabbalists' treasury
  of souls [[1]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-plato-phaedo-recollection) [[2]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-glanvill-souls-pre-existed) [[3]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-waite-zohar-treasury-of-souls).
- **It comes down**, partly or wholly, from the intelligible world: Plotinus, Proclus, Porphyry, the Hermetica
  [[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-plotinus-descent-voluntary) [[5]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-211-descends-whole) [[6]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-porphyry-soul-binds-itself).
- **It comes from the parents with the body** (traducianism): Tertullian [[7]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-tertullian-two-seeds-inseparable).
- **God makes it for this body**: Aquinas against pre-existence, Descartes's "expressly created"
  [[8]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-aquinas-soul-made-in-the-body) [[9]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-descartes-soul-expressly-created-not-pilot).
- **No one knows**, and saying so is a position: Augustine [[10]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-retractations-does-not-know-origin).
- **It begins with its body and is many only through bodies**: Avicenna [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-soul-begins-with-body).
- **It was never made**: the unborn ātman, the eternal puruṣas [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-katha-unborn-undying) [[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-sankhya-plurality-of-purushas).
- **It forms in stages at birth**, out of qi: po first, then hun [[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-zichan-po-first-then-hun).
- **It is a Spirit that incarnates many times**: Kardec [[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-kardec-soul-is-incarnate-spirit).

---

## A. Before the body: pre-existence and recollection

**The Phaedo's argument from learning.** Cebes recalls Socrates' saying that learning is recollection
(anamnēsis). If so, we must have learned before birth:

> "we must necessarily have learned in some previous time what we now remember. But this is impossible if our
> soul did not exist somewhere before being born in this human form" [[1]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-plato-phaedo-recollection)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTma6xEUveMD9g1W7k

What is remembered in the Phaedo is the Equal itself, a mathematical object. So pre-existence is argued from
knowing mathematics. The same dialogue's first argument is a cycle: the living come from the dead as the dead
from the living [[16]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-plato-phaedo-cyclical-argument). That proves only that souls persist, not that they
are eternal (see [06-survival.md](/explore/histories/soul/06-survival)).

**The Pythagorean memory of former lives.** Diogenes Laertius reports that Pythagoras claimed to remember
being Aethalides and then Euphorbus, with the gift of describing "the soul's wanderings—how it traveled into
various plants and animals" [[17]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-pythagoras-euphorbus-soul-wanderings) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhAwalpTYhD8XcOymxc.
This is a late compiler reporting a legend.

**The Cambridge Platonist revival.** Joseph Glanvill (*Lux orientalis*, 1662) defends the view "that our souls
were extant before these earthly bodies" [[2]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-glanvill-souls-pre-existed) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BfzzpNXCvXwMQW8BmjZ.
He says the objections show only that objectors cannot picture the earlier state. The book is in English.

**The treasury of souls (the guf).** In A. E. Waite's English of the Zohar (1902), the souls were hidden in
God's thought before the world, then stored:

> "He then gathered them into a treasury in the supernal garden of Eden, and that treasury is never filled"
> [[3]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-waite-zohar-treasury-of-souls) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeotkYYYtQwrIEEQW1S

The *Disputatio cabalistica de anima* (1635) has the same receptacle: "In the world of souls, however, they
dwell in a receptacle prepared for them" (*In mundo autem animarum versantur in receptaculo illis parato*)
[[18]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-disputatio-souls-created-before-world-receptacle) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bfo94617IDoXuC5Q0Sb.
The same text says the souls of the nations do not come from the same place as Israel's, citing the Zohar and
the Kuzari [[19]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-disputatio-zohar-kuzari-israel-holy-souls). Origin here also sorts peoples. Buddeus (1720)
reports the Lurianic form, a collective pre-existence in the first man: "They believe all souls existed together
in Adam, and fell along with him." (*& omnes simul in Adamo ex- itisse, & cum eo lapsas esse*)
[[20]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-buddeus-kabbalists-all-souls-in-adam) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BfuIKzkX8NN7fNQETAj.

## B. Descent: the soul comes down

The Platonists ask a different question. The soul's origin is not in doubt; it belongs above. The question is
why it came down, and how much of it did.

**Plotinus: the report, then the theodicy.** *Ennead* IV.8 opens with an experience, not an argument: "roused
from body, and converted to myself … I then perceive an admirable beauty" [[21]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-plotinus-iv8-roused-from-body)
(Taylor's English, 1794). Plotinus then reconciles the old accounts (exile, fall, the soul "sown" for the
universe's sake). Descent is free and not free at once:

> "nor the voluntary and yet involuntary condition of descent, by any means repugnant to the truth"
> [[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-plotinus-descent-voluntary) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bi8TVXMpLHijB36KakA

And not all of the soul comes down: "the whole of our soul also does not enter into body, but something
belonging to it always abides in the intelligible" [[22]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-plotinus-undescended-soul)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bi8TVXMpLHijB36KakL. Plotinus marks this as his own minority view.

**Proclus: all of it comes down, again and again.** "Every particular soul, descending into generation,
descends as a whole." (*Omnis particularis anima, descendens in generationem,*) [[5]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-211-descends-whole)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgUvVF7tfKHgyDbC4OR. A part that always thought without change would be
intellect, not soul [[23]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#neo-crit-whole-descent-against-undescended). Descent is also a law without end:

> "Every particular soul can descend into generation infinitely, and can ascend from generation to Being itself."
> [[24]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-206-descends-endlessly) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgUvVF7tfKHgyDbC4OL

**Iamblichus.** The usual view is that Proclus here follows Iamblichus against Plotinus. The Proclus page names
neither. Iamblichus' own *De anima* is not yet in the KB.

**Porphyry: the soul binds itself.** "For nature bound body in soul, but soul bound itself in body." (ψυχὴ δὲ
ἑαυτὴν ἐν σώματι) [[6]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-porphyry-soul-binds-itself) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bkp0wkqFODCsdJoXCIh. The
binding is the soul's own turning toward the passions, so only the soul can undo it.

**The Hermetica: a ladder up.** *Corpus Hermeticum* X.7 has souls rising through kinds: "others pass from the
water-dwellers into land-dwellers; the land-dwellers into winged creatures; and others pass from the airy
creatures into humans" [[25]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-hermetica-ch10-ladder-of-souls) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BejFoukEepZzy8QxT0A.
Here the human soul's origin is in lower souls, not in heaven.

## C. From the parents or from God: traducianism, creationism, and Augustine's refusal

**Tertullian: the soul is propagated with the body.** In *De anima* 27 (Holmes's printed English):

> "although we shall allow that there are two kinds of seed—that of the body and that of the soul—we still
> declare that they are inseparable, and therefore contemporaneous and simultaneous in origin."
> [[7]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-tertullian-two-seeds-inseparable) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhApeqgUU5RkZDU8VZe

This rests on a corporeal soul. Tertullian takes Zeno's syllogism ("the soul is a corporeal substance") and
Cleanthes' argument that children resemble parents in soul as well as body [[26]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-tertullian-enlists-zeno-cleanthes)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhApeqgUU5RkZDU8VZH. If the soul is a body, it can be inherited. The Latin term
of art is *de traduce*, "from the shoot"; a letter in Jerome's correspondence asks "whether that opinion is
rather to be held which says that the soul is de traduce" [[27]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-optatus-consultation-de-traduce)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhDwjoXWoHFvkVyuhRt.

**Augustine: I do not know.** Late in life Augustine records that he had not decided, and that he knew one
thing only:

> "I had confessed that I did not know whether they are propagated from the soul of the first man and thereafter
> from parents3 or whether they are assigned to individuals severally without propagation just as to the first one"
> [[10]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-retractations-does-not-know-origin) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bkp139NGt076H8bkvKb

What he did know was that the soul "is not body, but spirit", so he rejects Tertullian's grounds while leaving
Tertullian's conclusion open. A 1475 excerpt puts it personally: *Dico ego de anima mea nescio quomodo venerit in
corpus meum* ("I say concerning my soul, I do not know how it came into my body")
[[28]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-nescio-quomodo-venerit) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiPvE2e5mlUlTzlZhEB. He says he never
answered the question he put to Jerome [[29]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-letter-to-jerome-left-unexplained). What held him back
was original sin. Whatever the origin, "however it is that the origin of souls stands, whether they are
propagated from that [first] one or from no other", the Mediator's soul took no sin from Adam
[disputed] https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bh9WUWANpH9rINdGBE5. A new
soul made by God would be sinless; a soul from Adam would carry the sin. He could not choose without losing one
doctrine or the other.

**The three positions as a sceptic saw them.** Agrippa (1530) reports the "dissension": "some think that the
souls of all men were made in heaven at the origin of the world, among whom is one of many, the most learned
Origen" [[30]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-agrippa-reports-origin-of-souls-dispute) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhNfEIGSVotpWN6gCbN.

**Aquinas: made in the body.** Against the view that Adam's soul was made before his body, like the angels:

> "Since, therefore, the soul is the … proper act of the body, the soul was produced in the body."
> [[8]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-aquinas-soul-made-in-the-body) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiPwp560jwjz5r3SiHT

If the soul is the body's form, it cannot exist first and arrive later. That rules out Origen. That
creationism was the scholastic default is not yet a page-checked claim in the KB.

**Descartes: expressly created.** The rational soul "cannot be drawn from the power of matter":

> "it must be expressly created; and that it is not sufficient that it be lodged in the human body exactly like
> a pilot in a ship" [[9]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-descartes-soul-expressly-created-not-pilot) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bem5RoRnUr0TFVAeabA

Veitch's printed English. Everything else in the body comes from matter; only the soul needs a separate act.

## D. Avicenna: the soul begins with its body

Avicenna answers Plato directly. Souls are many only because bodies are many, so they cannot be many before
there are bodies. In the Latin *De anima* V.3:

> "It begins to exist with the body only." (*Singularitas ergo anima rum est aliquid quod esse incipit et non est
> eternum quod fuerit semper.*) [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-soul-begins-with-body) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiPvFJDMtTfiFzRGYEQ

The body is made as the soul's "kingdom and instrument". The text says "begins to exist with the body", not
"created from nothing". On the rūḥ the Qur'an gives a short answer: "The spirit comes at the bidding of my Lord,
and ye are given but a little knowledge thereof" (Palmer, 1880) [[31]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-quran-17-85-spirit-from-command)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BmiNye2tHmNIk3dxlF2. The verse is about rūḥ, not nafs. Al-Hujwīrī uses it against
those who call the spirit eternal and make it pass from person to person [[32]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-hujwiri-spirit-not-eternal).
For Sunni Sufism the spirit is created, not a part of God.

## E. Never made: the unborn self

The Upanishads turn the question down. The Kaṭha (Hume's English):

> "The wise one [i. e. the soul, the ātman, the self] is not born, nor dies." [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-katha-unborn-undying)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWpKOzEuBoNwN1Wnj

It came from nowhere and became no one. There is nothing to explain because nothing began. In the Chāndogya
the self is the ground of all: "That art thou" [[33]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-chandogya-tat-tvam-asi). Sāṃkhya keeps the eternity but
counts the selves: "it is proved that there is a plurality of souls" (Davies' "souls" for puruṣa)
[[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-sankhya-plurality-of-purushas) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsAVxUAM5NabODwEC. Many, eternal, none made.

The Buddhist answer has no self to begin. What goes into the womb is viññāṇa: "I have said that cognition is the
cause of name-and form" (Rhys Davids' English) [[34]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-mahanidana-vinnana-descends)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhPXKnYnAOyD1jZKTCy. The Tibetan bardo text says the consciousness-mind "has shown
its impermanence" in the same line that has it take another body [[35]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-bardo-tib-rnam-shes-takes-body).

## F. Formed at birth: po first, then hun

The Zuozhuan (535 BCE) puts the soul's origin inside the life of the body, as a sequence:

> 子產曰、能、人生始化曰魄、既生魄陽曰魂 [[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-zichan-po-first-then-hun) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlWFAjYWGMUOylWYg

In our English: at a person's birth the first transformation is called po; once po is born, its yang is called
hun. (Legge's printed English has po "the animal soul" and hun "the spirit" [[36]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-legge-hunpo-soul-and-spirit).) With
refined nourishment they grow strong until they reach shen ming. So the soul is not given whole; it is formed and
grows. Later glosses keep the order. The Xingli daquan (1415) has po form with the embryo and hun as its first
stirring: 故人之知覺屬魂形體屬魄, "knowing and perceiving belong to hun, the bodily frame to po"
[[37]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-xingli-knowing-hun-body-po) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bl0V1XtkG1LrwZq1DXi. A Qianlong treatise: 言夫人生之初魄聚而魂麗焉,
"at a person's beginning the po gathers and the hun attaches to it" [[38]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-lulu-zhengyi-po-gathers-hun-attaches).
The Huainanzi gives the stuff: heaven's qi is hun, earth's qi is po [[39]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-huainanzi-heaven-qi-hun-earth-qi-po).
The English
is ours; SL's English rotates its words for hun and po (see [07](/explore/histories/soul/07-soul-mind-spirit-life)).

## G. A pre-existent Spirit: Kardec

Kardec's *Livre des Esprits* (1857) makes the soul a Spirit in its incarnate state:

> "The qualities of the soul are those of the Spirit incarnated within us" (*Les qualités de l'âme sont celles de
> l'Esprit qui est incarné*) [[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-kardec-soul-is-incarnate-spirit) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOa0URRSoN17vcA8z4

The soul had its individuality before incarnation and keeps it after. It passes through progressive lives, never
in an animal. This is pre-existence and reincarnation in the language of the 1850s.

---

## Where the traditions disagree

- **Is there a "before"?** Plato, the Kabbalists, Glanvill and Kardec say yes. Aquinas and Avicenna say no:
  the soul is the body's form or begins with it. The Upanishads say the question is badly put.
- **One origin or a sorting?** The Kabbalist texts give Israel's souls a different source
  [[19]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-disputatio-zohar-kuzari-israel-holy-souls). Avicenna and Aquinas give every human soul the same one.
- **What does the answer protect?** For Augustine, original sin. For Plato, the knowledge of mathematics. For
  Avicenna, the individuality of each soul. For Tertullian, a bodily soul that can be inherited.
- **Given whole or grown?** The Chinese texts grow it (po, then hun, then shen ming). The Latin texts give a whole
  soul at one moment.
- **For the machine question:** on Tertullian's terms a soul is passed on by generation; on Descartes's it must
  be "expressly created"; on Avicenna's it begins with a fitting body. Only the last leaves room for a soul to
  begin with a new kind of body. Aristotle's objection that each soul needs "its own body" is in
  [[40]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-grk-each-soul-its-own-body). See page 08.

## Critiques

- **The Greek witnesses project.** Herodotus credits Egypt with a 3,000-year cycle through all animals that no
  Egyptian text teaches [[41]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-herodotus-ii123-transmigration) [[42]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#egy-crit-greek-readers-platonize-egypt).
- **"Where does the soul come from?" was also asked of the idea.** Tylor dates such speculation "back to the
  savage condition of our race" [[43]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-tylor-plural-souls-savage-condition), and Spencer derives the soul from
  a failure to tell sleep from death [[44]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-spencer-ghost-theory). Both explain a belief by an error of the
  believer [[45]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-ghost-and-external-soul-as-savage-inference) [[46]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-tylor-frame-shapes-world-glosses).
- **SL's English garbles Augustine's alternative.** The Latin offers "or created a new one, as for the first man";
  SL's English says "created a new one for the first man" (tagged `mistranslation`;
  [[28]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-nescio-quomodo-venerit)).
- **Plotinus' undescended soul blurs soul and intellect**, Proclus objects [[23]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#neo-crit-whole-descent-against-undescended).

## Open questions / what the canon reads would settle

- **Iamblichus, *De anima*** (Stobaeus I.49): the full-descent thesis in his own words.
- **Tertullian, *De anima* in Latin**, and **Peter Lombard, *Sentences* II d.17–18**, for creationism as the school
  default. Origen's own *De principiis* is not yet in the KB; we have him only
  through Agrippa.
- **Moses de León, *Sefer ha-Nefesh ha-Ḥakhamah*** and **Saadia, *Emunot ve-Deʿot* VI**.
- **Kardec's *Spirits' Book*** in English (held, unread).
- Whether the Hongmingji debate also argued about origin, not only survival.

title: 6. Does it survive death, and as what?
md:
**The question.** When a person dies, does anything go on? If so, what: a witless image, a judged heart, a
shade that must be fed, a part of the soul, a mind, a reborn stream, a resurrected person, or qi that scatters?
"Survival" is not one question. It splits into *whether* something persists, *how long*, *whether it is still
someone*, and *whether it remembers*.

**How to read it.** ✓ claims are verified on a Source Library page; ◐ claims are hedged ("reports"). Quotes are
SL's English (a model translation) unless the book is English or the original is given. All claims carry
`q:survival`. Where souls come from is [05](/explore/histories/soul/05-where-souls-come-from);
the fates of each soul in plural systems are on [09](/explore/histories/soul/09-many-souls).

**The short answer.**
- **A shade without wits or rest**: Homer's eidōlon, Sheol's rephaim, the hungry Mesopotamian ghost
  [[1]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-homer-eidola-of-men-outworn) [[2]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-dewette-rephaim-joyless-shades) [[3]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-jastrow-unburied-spirit-hunger).
- **A judged heart, and a ba that must rejoin the body**: Egypt [[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-bod-weighing-heart-feather) [[5]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-bod-ch89-soul-united-to-body).
- **The soul is immortal, or survives for a time**: Plato's Phaedo; the Stoics until the conflagration
  [[6]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-plato-phaedo-affinity) [[7]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-stoics-soul-connate-pneuma-survives-until-conflagration).
- **Nothing survives as a self**: Epicurus' scattered atoms, Fan Zhen's blade [[8]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-epicurus-soul-scattered-incorporeal-foolish) [[9]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-fanzhen-blade-sharpness).
- **Only what was perfected survives**: al-Fārābī, Gersonides, Porphyry's second death [[10]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-farabi-which-souls-survive) [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-porphyry-two-deaths).
- **The individual soul survives, and philosophy cannot prove it either way**: Avicenna vs Pomponazzi
  [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-soul-not-die-not-transmigrate) [[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-pomponazzi-immortality-neutral-problem).
- **It returns in another body**: gilgul, the Gītā, the Buddhist continuum "neither the same nor another"
  [[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-disputatio-gilgul-and-ibbur-two-species) [[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-milinda-lamp-neither-same-nor-other).
- **It disperses as qi, but stays continuous with the descendants**: Zhu Xi [[16]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-zhuxi-ancestor-qi-continuous).
- **It goes on in a subtler body**: the Neoplatonic vehicle, Swedenborg, Kardec, Theosophy [[17]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-196-perpetual-body) [[18]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-kardec-perispirit-semi-material-envelope).

---

## A. The shade: something survives, but not the person

**Homer.** Odysseus tries three times to hold his dead mother's psychē, and "thrice she flitted from my arms like
a shadow or a dream" [[19]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-homer-psyche-flits-like-shadow-dream) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTm1h9VQjlIWjZTUpf.
Achilles calls Hades the place where

> "unheeding dead dwell, the phantoms of men outworn" (ἀφραδέες ναίουσι, βροτῶν εἴδωλα καμόντων)
> [[1]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-homer-eidola-of-men-outworn) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTm1h9VQjlIWjZTUpw

The dead are eidōla and *aphradees*, without wits. In *Iliad* I the psychai go to Hades while the heroes
"themselves" (αὐτοὺς δὲ ἑλώρια τεῦχε κύνεσσιν) are left for the dogs [[20]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-homer-the-self-is-the-body): the
self is the body, and the psychē is what leaves it.

**Sheol.** De Wette (1813) describes the biblical dead as rephaim, "The state of the dead or shadows", a joyless
state, though with perception, like the shadows of the Greeks [[2]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-dewette-rephaim-joyless-shades)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhNfKkG5CW8yjEhHRgp. The mortalists' proof texts, as Menasseh ben Israel sets them out:
"In death there is no memory of you; in the pit, who shall praise you?" [[21]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-menasseh-mortalists-psalms-pit)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhtKrMILDlENNGngk6l. Qohelet asks whether man's ruach goes up and the beast's down;
"all have one spirit" [[22]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-eccl3-one-ruach-man-and-beast).

**Mesopotamia.** In Jastrow's Gilgamesh XII the uncared-for dead "is consumed by gnawing hunger, by a longing for
food" [[3]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-jastrow-unburied-spirit-hunger) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BihICEm3EtK2fXMvEPM. The land of
No-return is the house "Where dust is their sustenance, their food clay" [[23]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-descent-ishtar-dust-food)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BkAp5Hm0ngKYN4ycsau. An unrested ghost (ekimmu, now read eṭemmu) returns to fasten
on the living [[24]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-thompson-ekimmu-returns). Survival is real but dependent: the living must feed the dead.

**China's hungry dead are the same kind.** Zichan says those who die by violence 匹夫匹婦强死、其魂魄猶能馮依於人 (their
hun and po can still cling to people) [[25]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-zichan-violent-death-ghost) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlWFAjYWGMUOylWYg.
The Ming rite for lone souls says their 所依精魄未散 (essence-po has not dispersed) [[26]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-tushubian-lone-souls-jingpo).

## B. Egypt: the judged heart and the returning ba

In Budge's 1898 account the heart only has to *balance* the feather of Maat, not outweigh it
[[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-bod-weighing-heart-feather). The dead pleads with the heart as a witness who could turn on him: "O my
heart, my mother ; O my heart, my mother !" [[27]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-bod-ch30-my-heart-my-mother) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgxPfJ7J9DwYCJgeqE7.
He denies each sin before the Forty-two judges [[28]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-bod-negative-confession). A heart that fails goes to "the
monster Āmām" by the Balance [disputed]. Survival is not given. It is earned, and the failure is
annihilation.

The ba does not escape the body. Chapter 89 is "of causing the soul to be united to its body":

> "Grant thou that my soul may come unto me from wheresoever it may be." [[5]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-bod-ch89-soul-united-to-body)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgxPfJ7J9DwYCJgeqFH

Naville's "winged soul" leaves its tomb and returns to the mummy [[29]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-naville-1886-gefluegelte-seele). Budge
makes the akh, not the ba, the immortal part in one book [[30]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-budge-1911-vocab-khu-immortal), and the ba
"beyond all doubt" eternal in another [[31]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-budge-1913-ba-heart-soul).

## C. Greek philosophy: immortal, scattered, or for a while

**Plato.** The Phaedo argues from opposites: "the souls of the dead exist somewhere, whence they come back to
life" [[32]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-plato-phaedo-cyclical-argument) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTma6xEUveMD9g1W7i. Then from
affinity: "the divine is by nature fitted to rule and lead, and the mortal to obey and serve", so the soul is
like the divine and indissoluble [[6]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-plato-phaedo-affinity) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTma6xEUveMD9g1W8A.
Earlier, Alcmaeon argued it was immortal "in virtue of its ceaseless movement" [[33]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-alcmaeon-immortal-by-ceaseless-motion).

**Epicurus.** The soul is atoms, and it ends:

> "when the whole frame is broken up, the soul is scattered and no longer has the same powers as before, nor the
> same motions; hence it does not possess sentience either" (λυομένου τοῦ ὅλου ἀθροίσματος ἡ ψυχὴ διασπείρεται)
> [[8]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-epicurus-soul-scattered-incorporeal-foolish) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhAwalpTYhD8XcOyn20

Lucretius sets out to prove that minds and souls "are born and are mortal" [[34]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-lucretius-animos-rendered-spirits).

**The Stoics: for a time.** The soul is connate pneuma, a body:

> "from which they infer first that it is a body and secondly that it survives death. Yet it is perishable"
> [[7]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-stoics-soul-connate-pneuma-survives-until-conflagration) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhAwalpTYhD8XcOymwb

Cleanthes has all souls last until the conflagration; Chrysippus only the wise. A third option between Plato and
Epicurus: survival limited in time and graded by wisdom.

## D. Neoplatonists: two deaths and a body that never leaves

Plotinus poses survival as a question of identity: which part "is the man himself"
[[35]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-plotinus-iv7-which-part-is-the-man) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bi8TYwtni7t7sPx5onk. Porphyry splits death:

> "For death is twofold: one is known, with the body being loosed from the soul, the other is that of the
> philosophers, with the soul being loosed from the body" (Ὁ γοῦν θάνατος διπλοῦς) [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-porphyry-two-deaths)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bkp0wkqFODCsdJoXCIh

The second death is a practice before the first. Proclus adds that the soul is never bodiless. "Every soul that is
participated in uses a body that is primarily eternal" [[17]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-196-perpetual-body), an immaterial vehicle
that puts on and strips off tunics [[36]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-vehicle-impassive-same-shape) [[37]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-209-vehicle-tunics).
The Hermetic minds, freed, "immediately put on their own tunic, the fiery one" [[38]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-hermetica-ch10-fiery-tunic).
Synesius makes the vehicle thin or earthy by the soul's moral state [[39]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-synesius-vehicle-earthy-misrendered).

## E. Returning: gilgul, rebirth, and the continuum

**Gilgul.** The *Disputatio cabalistica* (1635): "The Jews believe that souls change bodies, or are revolved from
one body into another; the Pythagoreans call this Metempsychosis". It names two kinds, גלגול (gilgul) and עיבור
(ibbur) [[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-disputatio-gilgul-and-ibbur-two-species) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bfo94617IDoXuC5Q0a0. Gilgul is
a return to finish what the soul could not; ibbur is a righteous soul "poured into the soul of the living, like
light proceeding from light" [[40]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-disputatio-ibbur-righteous-soul-poured-in). The Zohar, in Ginsburg: "souls
revolve like a stone which is thrown from a sling", three times at most [[41]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-ginsburg-zohar-souls-slung-three-times).
It was contested inside Judaism: Saadia and Albo denied it, and Menasseh holds it proved from the Zohar
[[42]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-menasseh-saadia-albo-deny-zohar-proves); Maimonides denied it [[43]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-menasseh-maimonides-denied-abravanel-answers).

**India.** The Gītā: "so the embodied (self) casting off old bodies, goes to others and new ones" (Telang)
[[44]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-gita-dehin-changes-bodies) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlJ2PBx4HEq6FKsSD. The Jain jīva rises when cleaned
of karmic matter [[45]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-jain-karma-is-matter).

**The Buddhist answer.** Without a self, what is reborn? Nāgasena's lamp:

> "One comes into being, another passes away; and the rebirth is, as it were, simultaneous. Thus neither as the
> same nor as another does a man go on" [[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-milinda-lamp-neither-same-nor-other) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRlBroc5VJM6ITuBOk

The tradition states the objection itself: if the aggregates are not the self, who experiences the deeds' results
[[46]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-tengyur-who-experiences-karma)? The Kathāvatthu refutes those who made the person ultimately real
[[47]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-kathavatthu-puggala-ultimate-reality).

**Resurrection.** Survival can also be the return of the body. Abravanel holds that at the resurrection each soul
returns to its first body [[43]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-menasseh-maimonides-denied-abravanel-answers). Averroes finds "the return of the soul
to other bodies" free of the absurdities of the same bodies returning [[48]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-averroes-soul-returns-in-other-bodies).
Al-Ghazālī's Tahāfut ends by "refuting their denial of bodily resurrection" [[49]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-ghazali-tahafut-18-20-soul-and-resurrection).
Stillingfleet makes the risen body the same "Not from the Consciousness of the Soul, but from that Life which is
the Result of the Union of the Soul and Body" [[50]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-stillingfleet-body-identity-not-consciousness). A Christian
patristic text on the resurrection itself is not yet in the KB.

## F. Conditional, individual, or unprovable: the Islamic and Latin debate

**Only the perfected.** In Dieterici's German of al-Fārābī, souls of the ignorant cities "bedürfen dieselben zu
ihrem Bestehn notwendig des Stoffs" (need matter in order to exist), and perish with it [[10]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-farabi-which-souls-survive)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BmiNukILiokqVv8wELe. Abraham Shalom reports Gersonides' view that a man without
intellectual development dies "like the death of an animal" ◐ [[51]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-neveh-shalom-gersonides-death-like-animal).

**Every individual.** Avicenna, *Shifāʾ* V.4: "On the human soul not perishing nor transmigrating" (في ان النفس
الانسانية لا تفسد ولا تناسخ) [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-soul-not-die-not-transmigrate) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhibVye1RH7VxgfG0r3.
What dies with another depends on it; the soul does not. The c. 1500 Latin heading is misread in SL's English
[[52]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-latin-definit-misread).

**Lateran V and Pomponazzi.** In 1513 the council condemned those "asserentes, Animam intellectivam mortalem
esse aut unicam in cunctis hominibus" [[53]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-lateran-v-apostolici-regiminis) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhI8qAygmY6DpB6l1Dl,
and ordered philosophers to refute them. Three years later Pomponazzi:

> "the question of the immortality of the soul  is a neutral problem, just like the question of the eternity of
> the world" (*quæstio de im- mortalitate animæ est neutrum problema*) [[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-pomponazzi-immortality-neutral-problem)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bf1JQeD4alZVhlkqOIv

No natural reason compels either conclusion. Descartes later offers his proof as obedience to the council
[[54]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-descartes-invokes-lateran-v). Aquinas reportedly devotes eight articles to how the separated soul can know ◐
[[55]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-aquinas-separated-soul-question).

## G. Eternal, not immortal; simple, not provably lasting

**Spinoza.** "The human Mind cannot be absolutely destroyed with the Body, but something of it remains which is
eternal." [[56]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-spinoza-something-eternal-remains) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BembIQgFKlHjuxOPOMm. The
demonstration denies it any duration in time. Eternal is not immortal.

**Mendelssohn and Kant.** Mendelssohn's Socrates argues that nature cannot pass from being to non-being "without
transition" [[57]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-mendelssohn-no-middle-being-nonbeing) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bht7MmgnHqVUeyNMVuk, and Wolff
that a simple substance cannot perish as composites do [[58]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-wolff-731-simple-substance-cannot-perish). Kant
answers in B (1787), under the heading "Widerlegung des Mendelssohnschen Beweises der Beharrlichkeit der Seele":
a simple soul can still fade by degrees [[59]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-mod-kant-remissio-against-simplicity-proofs). In A he states the
third paralogism, "Whatever is conscious of the numerical identity of its self at different times is, to that
extent, a person", and denies it proves a persisting subject [[60]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-kant-third-paralogism-personality)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhBfftzER8zvrziRjIz. Mendelssohn's own residual doubt is whether God keeps the Geist
awake after death [[61]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-mendelssohn-simple-soul-sleep-doubt).

## H. Qi disperses: Neo-Confucian survival as lineage

The Liji: hun-qi returns to heaven, form-po to earth [[62]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-liji-hunqi-heaven-xingpo-earth). Zhu Xi: 鬼神只是氣
(gui and shen are only qi) [[63]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-zhuxi-guishen-only-qi) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bl0Z7VrdSkq9cVOvXbZ. Yet the
ancestors can be reached, because 蓋祖考之氣與己連續, the ancestors' qi is continuous with one's own
[[16]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-zhuxi-ancestor-qi-continuous) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bl0Z7VrdSkq9cVOvXd6. Not individual immortality,
and not nothing. Gu Yanwu reads "wandering hun" as passing from something to nothing, against rebirth
[[64]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-guyanwu-youhun-not-rebirth).

**Fan Zhen vs Huiyuan.** Huiyuan: 火之傳於 薪猶神之傳於形, as fire passes to firewood so spirit passes to body, and on
to other bodies [[65]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-huiyuan-fire-firewood) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bl0acp426HOdHuP3z9q. Fan Zhen's *Shenmie
lun*: spirit is to body as sharpness to a blade, 然而捨利無刃捨刃無利未聞刃没而利存豈容形亡 而神在 [[9]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-fanzhen-blade-sharpness)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bl0ad19SZvZr6DQymMF: no one has heard of the blade gone and the sharpness left.
(Our English; SL has none.) The court took the side of survival [[66]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-shenyue-spirit-originally-imperishable).

## I. Spiritualist and Theosophical survival

Swedenborg: the dead man "enters the spiritual world and puts on a spiritual body" [[67]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-swedenborg-spiritual-body)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BeotMNhbb4VEgBH2MSL. Kardec's spirit wears a *périsprit*, changed like clothing between
worlds [[18]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-kardec-perispirit-semi-material-envelope). Blavatsky puts the dead in Kama-loka, "the limbus of
scholastic theology, the Hades of the ancients" [[68]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-blavatsky-kamaloka-astral-eidolon); Leadbeater counts "no
less than three corpses" [[69]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-leadbeater-three-corpses). Myers rests the survival case on a "subliminal Self"
[[70]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-myers-subliminal-self); Bergson's foreword has the body intervene only in the last plane of memory
[[71]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-bergson-body-intervenes-last-plane).

---

## Where the traditions disagree

- **Does the survivor think?** Homer: no. The Phaedo and Avicenna: yes, better than before
  [[72]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-compendium-separated-soul-understands). Mendelssohn: perhaps it sleeps.
- **Does it need a body?** Egypt, the resurrection texts, Proclus and Kardec: yes, its own or a subtle one.
  Plutarch's Platonic Osiris and Avicenna: no.
- **Is it earned?** Egypt, al-Fārābī, Gersonides and Chrysippus say survival depends on what you became. Avicenna
  and Lateran V say every rational soul lasts.
- **Is it someone?** The Buddhist lamp and Zhu Xi's qi keep continuity without a persisting self. Gilgul even
  can change who a man is: a sinner's changed soul can cost him his destined spouse (Knorr's Lurianic text) [[73]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-knorr-revolutionibus-women-spouse-souls).

## Critiques

- **The memory criterion presupposes what it explains.** Butler: "Consciousness of personal Identity presupposes,
  and therefore cannot constitute, personal Identity" [[74]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-em-butler-consciousness-presupposes-identity); Leibniz
  adds outside signs [[75]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-leibniz-consciousness-not-only-means).
- **A council can command assent, not a proof** [[76]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-chr-lateran-cannot-command-a-proof).
- **Al-Ghazālī: the immateriality proofs are not demonstrative** (as Marmura summarises) [[77]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#isl-crit-ghazali-immateriality-not-demonstrated).
- **Back-projection.** The Life of Homer made the flitting shade "the soul is immortal" [[78]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-backproj-life-of-homer-immortal-soul).
  Budge heads Pyramid Texts "The Doctrine of Eternal Life" [[79]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-backproj-budge-doctrine-of-eternal-life)
  [[80]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-egypt-eternal-life-and-heaven). Greeks put Egypt's dead in Hades [[81]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#egy-crit-greek-readers-platonize-egypt).
  "Immortal soul" for nefesh fails: the Zohar leaves the nefesh "in the tomb as long as there are bones"
  [[82]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-duhem-zohar-nefesh-stays-in-tomb) [[83]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-heb-immortal-soul-is-not-nefesh). "Transmigration" flattens
  gilgul, ibbur and gilgul meḥilot [[84]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-heb-gilgul-is-not-metempsychosis). "The soul" flattens hun and po,
  which part in opposite directions [[85]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#chn-crit-soul-flattens-hun-po).
- **Fan Zhen's critics are weak.** Xiao Chen's dull blade only shows sharpness can go first [[86]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#chn-crit-xiaochen-dull-blade).

## Open questions / what the canon reads would settle

- unverified: Locke's own II.27 (the prince and the cobbler) [unverified]; needs OCR.
- Al-Ghazālī's Discussions 18–20 and Averroes' reply on resurrection.
- Pomponazzi chs. 8–14 and Contarini's reply; Gregory of Nyssa on the resurrection.
- Bergson, *L'âme et le corps*, and Rohde's *Psyche*.
- The Pyramid Texts themselves, not through Budge.

title: 7. How do soul, mind, spirit and life differ?
md:
**The question.** English has four words, soul, mind, spirit and life, and uses them loosely. Every tradition
in this KB also has several words, but it does not cut the field at the same places. Which word names what
lives, what thinks, what breathes, and what survives? Where does each tradition draw its lines? And where does
English (SL's, or a printed translator's) move them?

**How to read it.** ✓ claims are verified on a Source Library page. Quotes are SL's English (a model
translation) unless the book is English or the original is given. Claims carry `q:soul-mind-spirit-life`.
Two boundaries belong to sister KBs: soul and **intellect** (nous, ʿaql, buddhi, the agent intellect) is
nous-kb's; soul and **life** (Aristotle's ladder, and how "soul" and "life" came apart in the 17th century) is
aliveness-kb's (its page 04, section D). This page links them and does not repeat them.

**The short answer.**
- **Greek: psychē is what leaves, noos is what knows, pneuma is a body, life can be apart from soul.**
  [[9]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-homer-circe-noos-stays-in-swine) [[10]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-pythagoreans-soul-distinct-from-life) [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#neo-crit-spirit-merges-three-words).
- **Latin: anima lives, animus and mens think, spiritus is breath or the incorporeal.** Lucretius makes animus and
  anima one; Gassendi finds Descartes "addressing only the mind" [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-lucretius-animos-rendered-spirits) [[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-gassendi-mind-not-soul).
- **Hebrew: nefesh is the living person, ruach the breath beasts share, neshamah the intellect.**
  [[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-exod15-seventy-nefesh-counts-persons) [[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-eccl3-one-ruach-man-and-beast) [[16]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-disputatio-neshamah-true-intellect).
- **Arabic and Persian: nafs is the self, often the lower self; rūḥ is from God's command; qalb is the heart that
  knows.** [[17]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-hujwiri-nafs-source-of-evil) [[18]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-quran-17-85-spirit-from-command) [[19]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-ibntufayl-three-senses-of-heart).
- **Sāṃkhya: the self (puruṣa) only watches; buddhi, the intellect, is on the side of matter.** [[20]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-sankhya-stranger-appears-agent).
- **Chinese: hun and po are defined by what they go with, shen and jing; xin takes charge.** [[21]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-lingshu-benshen-hun-po-defined).
- **German: Seele and Geist are two stages, and English needs three words for them.** [[22]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-render-geist-spirit-or-mind-hegel) [[23]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-jung-seele-vs-psyche).
- **The modern exit: no soul, only the thinking.** James: "the passing Thought itself is the only verifiable
  thinker" [[24]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-james-passing-thought-only-thinker).

---

## A. Greek: psychē, nous, thymos, pneuma

**In Homer they are separate organs of the person.** Psychē is what goes to Hades. Thymos is the feeling breath
of the chest. Noos is what knows. Circe's swine keep their noos through a change of body:

> "They took on the heads, the voice, the bristles, and the physical shape of swine, yet their minds remained
> unchanged, just as they were before." [[9]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-homer-circe-noos-stays-in-swine) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTm1h9VQjlIWjZTUp3

What carries the person here is mind, not soul. SL's English renders thymos once as "spirit" and once as "life"
on one Odyssey page, and psychē as "spirit" four lines later [[25]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-homer-thymos-rendered-spirit-and-life). On one
Iliad page psychē is "life" (nothing "is not worth my life") and, seven lines on, "spirit" [[26]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-render-psyche-life-and-spirit-iliad9)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTkqThMnA2B85YrqET. Three Greek words, one English word; one Greek word, two English words.

**Philosophy redraws the lines.** The Pythagorean notes in Diogenes Laertius split soul from life outright:

> "All things live which partake of heat—this is why plants are living things—but all do not have a soul. The
> soul is a detached part of aether" [[10]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-pythagoreans-soul-distinct-from-life) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhAwalpTYhD8XcOymxx

Life is heat; soul is aether. The same notes divide the psychē into nous, phrenes and thymos, and put only the
phrenes beyond death [[27]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-pythagoreans-nous-phrenes-thymos-heart-brain). Democritus, Aristotle says, "roundly
identifies soul and mind" [[28]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-democritus-soul-and-mind-identical) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bkp1LfgqJZJGMHrwQhQ.
Aëtius makes the self-moving number a self-moving intellect: "taking "number" to stand for "intellect.""
(τὸν δ' ἀριθμὸν ἀντὶ τοῦ νοῦ παραλαμβάνει) [[29]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-aetius-pythagoras-number-moving-itself) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhD0tyWfEXb66hzf2ON.
Aristotle's predecessors marked soul by "movement and sensation" [[30]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-aristotle-predecessors-movement-and-sensation).

**The Neoplatonists rank them.** Proclus makes soul and life one property: "Every Soul is both life and that which
lives." (*Omnis Anima est et vita, et id, quod vivit.*) [[31]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-189-self-living) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgUvVF7tfKHgyDbC4Nt.
But soul is not intellect: a part that always thought without change would be nous, so the whole soul descends
[[32]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-211-descends-whole) [[33]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#neo-crit-whole-descent-against-undescended). In *Corpus Hermeticum* X.17 the
order is mind, then soul, then pneuma: the mind takes the soul as its wrapping, and the soul is borne in pneuma.
SL's English inverts it ("It took on a passible body like a cloak for the soul") [[34]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-hermetica-ch10-vestures-misrendered)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BejFoukEepZzy8QxT0F. When nous becomes a daimōn, SL writes "spirit" for δαίμων
[[35]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-hermetica-ch10-daimon-rendered-spirit).

**Zōē** (life as such, against bios) is not yet a claim of its own in this KB.

## B. Latin: anima, animus, mens, spiritus

**Lucretius makes two words one.** He sets out to prove that *animos animasque leves* are born and mortal, and asks
for one name for both. SL's English writes "spirits":

> "so that you may know that the spirits and the light souls are born and are mortal" (*Nunc age natiuos
> animantibus, et mortales Esse animos, animasque leues ut noscere possis*) [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-lucretius-animos-rendered-spirits)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BjbyLU3RnAH6FFZmGF2

Animus is mind (Lucretius glosses it *consilium*). "Spirits" imports the Christian spiritus.

**Augustine: mens is not a body.** The mind knows it is, lives and understands, but is not sure whether it is air
or fire, "Therefore, it is in no way some body." [[36]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-mind-certain-of-itself-not-body)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bkp1OqOoA1dVafaCYRP. Its trinity is memory, understanding and will
[[37]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-trinity-memory-understanding-will). When Augustine calls the soul "spirit", he means incorporeal
[[38]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-retractations-does-not-know-origin).

**Aquinas joins them again.** The soul, "the first principle of life", "is not a body but the act of a body"
[[39]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-aquinas-soul-not-body-but-act-of-body) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiPwp560jwjz5r3SiGP. And the intellect
itself is the form of the body [[40]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-aquinas-intellect-is-form-of-body). One form does the living and the knowing.

**Gassendi sees the split happen.** Descartes concluded he was "mens, sive animus, intellectus, ratio". Gassendi:

> "I thought I was addressing the human soul —that internal principle by which a human being lives, senses, moves
> from place to place, and understands. Instead, I find I was addressing only the mind ." (*Existimabam enim me
> alloqui animam humanam, seu internũ illud principium, quo homo viuit,*) [[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-gassendi-mind-not-soul)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bf1JGWG33XE1qAuO7h7

Anima (the principle of life) became mens (the thinking thing). The rest went to the body's machine; aliveness-kb
tells that story ([[1]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#soul-wd-descartes-functions-without-soul),
[[2]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-descartes-death-body-decays-not-soul-leaves)). Descartes still holds he is "very closely joined
to it and, as it were, intermingled with it" [[41]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-descartes-not-sailor-in-ship). In French he writes esprit and âme
for one thing, and SL renders "mind" and "soul" [[42]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-render-esprit-mind-ame-soul-descartes)
[[43]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-render-ame-senses-descartes-dioptrique). Spinoza writes mens, never anima [[44]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-spinoza-mind-idea-of-body).

**After the split the ladder gets longer.** Swedenborg: "There are therefore a superior mind and an inferior mind
(or mind properly so called)", with the soul's life further in still [[45]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-swedenborg-superior-inferior-mind)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgxPmjI0aIpgaf4mSmo. More's "spirits" are subtle matter, not souls
[[46]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-more-phantasm-soul-fabric-spirit-of-nature). Havenreuter's 1591 *ΨΥΧΟΛΟΓΙΑ sive philosophica de animo* renders
psychē as animus [[47]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-havenreuter-psychologia-de-animo). Wolff's anima and animus both come out "soul" in SL's
English [[48]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-wolff-empirical-vs-rational-psychology).

## C. Hebrew: nefesh, ruach, neshamah

**Nefesh counts living people.** "And all the souls that emerged from the thigh of Jacob were seventy souls" (כָּל נֶפֶשׁ
יֹצְאֵי יֶרֶךְ יַעֲקֹב שִׁבְעִים נָפֶשׁ) [[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-exod15-seventy-nefesh-counts-persons) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiFm0ilKGU0npyYuAEg.
SL's "souls" follows the KJV; the Hebrew counts persons. Genesis 2:7 has man become a *nefesh ḥayyah* when God
breathes the *nishmat ḥayyim* into him ([[3]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-gen27-nishmat-hayyim-nefesh-hayyah)). Pagnini's
thesaurus gives nefesh as anima, animus, the whole man, the body, the will ([[4]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-pagnini-nefesh-soul-mind-body-will)).

**Ruach is shared with beasts.** "and all have one spirit" (וְרוּחַ אֶחָד לַכֹּל) [[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-eccl3-one-ruach-man-and-beast)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiFm0ilKGU0npyYuAqT.

**Neshamah is intellect.** Moses de León, quoted in the *Disputatio* (1635):

> "The nature of the true intellect, hewn from the source of life and from the spring of intellect and wisdom,
> comes to establish its glory within the body" (עניין השכל האמיתי אשר ממקור החיים נחצב) [[16]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-disputatio-neshamah-true-intellect)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bfo94617IDoXuC5Q0YW

This is the soul–mind seam in a Kabbalist's own definition; nous-kb owns the intellect side. The Zohar says the three
"are all one in one" ([[5]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-zohar-nefesh-ruach-neshamah-all-one)), but sends them to three places at
death [[49]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-myer-zohar-ruach-garden-neshamah-returns) [[50]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-duhem-zohar-nefesh-stays-in-tomb). Menasseh's book
named for Gen 2:7's breath, *Nishmat Ḥayyim*, argues "the survival of the pure soul through the intellect"
[[51]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-menasseh-nishmat-hayyim-survival-by-intellect).

## D. Arabic and Persian: nafs, rūḥ, qalb, ʿaql

**Nafs is the self, and often the lower self.** Al-Hujwīrī: some take nafs for the spirit, some for the body or
blood, but the masters "agree that the reality of it is the source of evil and the basis of wickedness" (گروهی نفس
بمعنی روح است) [[17]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-hujwiri-nafs-source-of-evil) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTYRRbnqInviUqjgeG. Macdonald reports
al-Ghazālī's two usages: the soul that commands to evil, and the nafs that is "the very essence of man which knows
God" [[52]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-ghazali-two-senses-of-nafs).

**Rūḥ comes from the command.** Qur'an 17:85 is about the rūḥ, not the nafs [[18]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-quran-17-85-spirit-from-command).

**Qalb has three senses.** Ibn Ṭufayl:

> "I do not mean by the "heart" the physical heart, nor the spirit in its cavity, but I mean the form of that
> spirit overflowing with its powers upon the human body." [[19]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-ibntufayl-three-senses-of-heart) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BijWMYoRxgM52PNK0TE

The organ, the hot vapour (rūḥ) in it, and its form. In Homes's English of al-Ghazālī, "The spirit, for example,
which we call heart" has no size or divisibility [[53]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-ghazali-heart-spirit-no-quantity): spirit, heart and soul
are one thing under three words.

**The self is not the body.** Avicenna's floating man affirms his *dhāt* (self) but no limb, "nor heart, nor blood"
[[54]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-flying-man-not-heart-blood) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhibVye1RH7VxgfG0pL. The Latin print reads
"nor the soul, nor the brain" [[55]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-avicenna-flying-man-latin-animum). ʿAql, the intellect and the ladder of
intellects, is nous-kb's ([[6]](/explore/histories/nous/claims/islamic#isl-farabi-acquired-intellect)).

## E. Sāṃkhya and the Upanishads: the self is not the mind

In Sāṃkhya the knower does nothing and the thinker knows nothing:

> "from the activity of the modes the stranger (the soul) appears to be an agent." [[20]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-sankhya-stranger-appears-agent)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsAVxUAM5NabODwEF

Davies' "stranger" renders udāsīna, the one sitting apart. Buddhi (intellect) is on the side of prakṛti, matter;
nous-kb has the split ([[7]](/explore/histories/nous/claims/indian#ind-sankhya-split), [[8]](/explore/histories/nous/claims/indian#ind-sankhya-buddhi-adhyavasaya)). In the Kaṭha the
ātman rides; buddhi drives and manas is the reins: "Know thou the soul (ātman, self) as riding in a chariot"
[[56]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-katha-chariot-soul) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTWpKOzEuBoNwN1Wnl. In the Bṛhadāraṇyaka the ātman is "the
unseen Seer, the unheard Hearer, the unthought Thinker" [[57]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-brihad-unseen-seer) and can be said only as *neti,
neti* [[58]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-brihad-neti-neti). Nyāya, by contrast, makes the ātman a substance known by its marks, desire to
cognition (इच्छा द्वेष प्रयत्न सुख दुख ज्ञान ये सब आत्मा के लक्षण हैं) [[59]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-nyaya-marks-of-atman). The Milindapañha
denies a vedagū, an inner viewer at the window [[60]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-milinda-vedagu-living-principle).

## F. Chinese: hun, po, shen, xin

The Lingshu defines by what each goes with:

> 兩精相搏謂之神隨神徃來者謂之魂並 [[21]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-lingshu-benshen-hun-po-defined) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgScEx7echo27DLrMZK

When two essences clash it is shen; what comes and goes with shen is hun; what goes in and out with jing is po; what
takes charge of things is xin, the heart-mind (our English). Zhu Xi gives memory to po, the bodily one: 凡能記憶皆魄之所藏受也
[[61]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-zhuxi-po-stores-hun-issues) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bl0Z6vbM1oIUBaHWrlp. Zheng Xuan glosses breathing as
qi (hun) and the sharpness of ear and eye as po [[62]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-liji-jiyi-qi-shen-po-gui). Knowing goes to hun, the frame to
po [[63]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-xingli-knowing-hun-body-po). Gao You calls both "shen", so shen is a genus here, not a third soul
[[64]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-huainanzi-heaven-qi-hun-earth-qi-po). Legge's English makes po "the animal soul" and hun "the spirit", which
collides with 神 [[65]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-legge-hunpo-soul-and-spirit).

## G. German: Seele and Geist

Mendelssohn switches word when the question becomes conscious survival: Seele for the simple substance, Geist for
what may stay awake [[66]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-mendelssohn-simple-soul-sleep-doubt). Kant: "the thinking I, the soul" (*das denkende Ich,
die Seele*) is a name for the transcendental object of inner sense, which "has no application that extends to actual
objects" [[67]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-kant-soul-name-for-transcendental-object) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhBfftzER8zvrziRjIz. Hegel's
Geist is "Spirit" in one SL book and "Mind" in another [[22]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-render-geist-spirit-or-mind-hegel). Hartmann's Seele
is "soul" and seelisch "mental" [[68]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-render-seele-geist-hartmann); Fechner's Geist is "mind" and Seele "soul"
on facing scans [[69]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-fechner-render-geist-mind-seele-soul). Jung narrows Seele to a part:

> "Unter Psyche verstehe ich die Gesamtheit aller psychischen Vorgänge, der bewussten sowohl wie der unbewussten."
> [[23]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-jung-seele-vs-psyche) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgTYXY1ajgQGOcYDwVa

Psyche is the whole; Seele is a delimited function-complex, best called a personality.

## H. The modern exit: psychology without a soul

Brentano reports the phenomenalist slogan: "Ein Seele gibt es nicht, wenigstens nicht für uns", and Lange's "eine
Psychologie ohne Seele" [[70]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-brentano-lange-psychology-without-soul) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhD37xNzNG7tO00ZQoq.
James brackets the Soul for psychology:

> "Meanwhile, as psychologists, we need not be metaphysical at all. The phenomena are enough, the passing Thought
> itself is the only verifiable thinker" [[24]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-james-passing-thought-only-thinker) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgObDWupqDSCBEkPQ3n

The continuous thing is now a stream: "It is nothing jointed; it flows." [[71]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-james-stream-of-thought). La Mettrie
had already called the soul "only a vain term" for "the part within us that thinks" [[72]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-lamettrie-soul-vain-term).

---

## Where the traditions disagree

- **Does soul include mind?** Aristotle and Aquinas: yes, one form. Sāṃkhya: the self is not the intellect at all.
  Proclus: soul is below nous. Descartes: soul *is* mind.
- **Does soul include life?** Proclus and Aquinas: soul is life. The Pythagorean notes: plants live without soul.
  Descartes: life is the machine's (aliveness-kb).
- **Is "spirit" higher or lower?** Rūḥ is from God's command; Stoic and Neoplatonic pneuma is a fine body; More's
  spirits are matter; Hegel's Geist is above Seele. One English word, opposite places.
- **Where is memory?** Augustine puts it in the mind's trinity; Zhu Xi in po, the bodily soul.

## Critiques

- **"Soul" is not a stable rendering even of one word** on SL's pages [[73]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-soul-one-word-many-renderings).
  The far languages are not the only problem; Descartes, Hartmann and Hegel show it at home [[74]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-vernacular-soul-spirit-mind).
- **"Spirit" merges pneuma, ochēma and daimōn** [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#neo-crit-spirit-merges-three-words).
- **Etymology is not meaning.** Tylor's table runs nephesh, ruach, psychē and anima all back to "breath"
  [[75]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-tylor-breath-words-table); on the pages they have left breath in different directions
  [[76]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-etymology-is-not-meaning).
- **Five Indian words become "soul"**: ātman, puruṣa, jīva, dehin, vedagū/puggala [[77]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-ind-soul-renders-five-words)
  [[78]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-render-atman-self-vs-soul) [[79]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-render-jiva-ghoshal-refuses-soul) [[80]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-render-dehin-spiritus-spirit)
  [[81]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-render-puggala-no-soul).
- **Egypt: ka, ba and akh drift** between "double", "genius", "soul", "Heart-soul" and "Spirit-soul"
  [[82]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#egy-crit-soul-for-ba-unstable) [[83]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-budge-1913-ka-genius-or-double) [[84]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-budge-1913-khu-spirit-soul).
- **Consciousness is not soul.** The machine texts ask about mind and origination; the older definitions put soul
  in self-motion, self-knowledge or form [disputed] [[85]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-butler-new-phase-of-mind)
  [[86]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-lovelace-engine-originates-nothing). See page 08.

## Open questions / what the canon reads would settle

- **Pseudo-Augustine, *De anima et spiritu***, the medieval text that equated anima, spiritus, mens and animus
  (held and translated).
- **Gassendi's *Syntagma* De anima**: the corporeal anima of animals vs the incorporeal mens of man.
- **Melanchthon and Goclenius** on *psychologia*.
- unverified: Carus's opening line on the unconscious [unverified] needs the Introduction scans.
- Zōē vs bios, and pneuma as the Pauline third part, are not yet claims here.

title: 8. Could a machine have a soul?
md:
**The question.** Every tradition here defined the soul long before anyone built a machine that talks. So the
question must be translated: on *this* tradition's definition, what would a machine need? And what did the tradition
say about made things: statues, axes, golems, automata, men of wood?

**How to read it.** ✓ verified on a Source Library page; ◐ partial (hedged); ○ unverified, never quoted. Quotes are SL's English (a model translation of the page) unless the note says the English is printed
(Oxford Aristotle, Scott's Asclepius, Taylor's Plotinus, Veitch's Descartes, Rhys Davids, Davies, Lovelace, Butler)
or ours. Claims in double brackets are in this KB. Claims in sister KBs are written `nous-kb:<id>` or
`aliveness-kb:<id>`. The many-souls traditions (Nahua, Yoruba, Māori and others) are on
[09-many-souls](/explore/histories/soul/09-many-souls); this page uses only their artifacts.

**The short answer.**
- **No, by definition: the soul belongs to a natural or created thing, and a machine is neither.** Aristotle's axe,
  Aquinas's form of a body, Descartes's soul that "must be expressly created" [[1]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-aristotle)
  [[2]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-descartes) [[3]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-aquinas-soul-not-body-but-act-of-body).
- **No, because a body cannot turn back on itself or see itself.** Proclus, Mamertus, Avicenna, Plotinus
  [[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-186-self-reversion-incorporeal) [[5]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-mamertus) [[6]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-avicenna-floating-man)
  [[7]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-plotinus-iv7-not-atoms).
- **Only if it moves itself.** Xenocrates' self-moving number, Alcmaeon's ceaseless motion, Pico's self-shaping,
  Lovelace's "originate" [[8]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-xenocrates-self-moving-number) [[9]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-pico)
  [[10]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-lovelace-engine-originates-nothing).
- **Yes, but as a house, not a source.** The Asclepius's statues, the Egyptian ka, the golem: the soul comes from
  outside [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-hermetic) [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-egypt-ka-statue) [[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-golem)
  [[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-mach-ensouled-artifacts-are-not-precedents).
- **Yes, because "soul" names what organised matter does.** Epicurus, La Mettrie, Fan Zhen (◐), Butler
  [[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-epicurus-soul-scattered-incorporeal-foolish) [[16]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-lamettrie) [[17]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-fanzhen-sharpness)
  [[18]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-butler).
- **The question dissolves: nobody has one.** Nāgasena's chariot [[19]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-milinda-chariot).
- **Everything but the one that matters.** Sāṃkhya and the Jains put intellect on matter's side and consciousness
  in a substance no arrangement makes [[20]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-sankhya-witness) [[21]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-jain-niyamasara-only-conscious-substance).

---

## The table

"Needs" is what a machine would need *on that definition*. "On artifacts" is what the tradition's own text says
about made things; where the KB has nothing, the cell says so. The verdict is the tradition's.

| Tradition | Its soul (quoted) | A machine would need | On artifacts | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Homer (Odyssey XI) | the dead mother's psychē: "thrice she flitted from my arms like a shadow or a dream" [[22]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-homer-psyche-flits-like-shadow-dream) | something that leaves it at death and goes on as an image; the self is the body [[23]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-homer-the-self-is-the-body) | not yet in the KB | the question does not arise: psychē is what a living man loses |
| Alcmaeon, Thales (via Aristotle, Aëtius) | immortal "in virtue of its ceaseless movement" [[24]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-alcmaeon-immortal-by-ceaseless-motion) | motion that never stops and starts from itself | none in KB | open; turns on "self-" |
| Xenocrates | "a self-moving number" [[25]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-xenocrates-self-moving-number-compound); "the ousia of the soul to be a number moved by itself" [[26]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-plutarch-xenocrates-ousia-number-moved-by-itself) | to be a number that moves itself, not one moved by something else [[8]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-xenocrates-self-moving-number) | none; Aristotle's objection (moving units trace lines, so are bodies) is the nearest [[27]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-grk-number-soul-collapses-into-atoms) | turns on where the motion starts |
| Aristotle (De anima II.1) | first actuality of a natural body "having in itself the power of setting itself in movement and arresting itself" [[1]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-aristotle) | to be a *natural* body with its own principle of moving and stopping | the axe: if it were a natural body its whatness "would have been its essence, and so its soul … As it is, … it is just an axe" [[28]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-aristotle-axe-would-have-soul) (Oxford English) | no, by the word "natural" |
| Epicurus | atoms; at death "the soul is scattered and no longer has the same powers as before" [[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-epicurus-soul-scattered-incorporeal-foolish) | the right arrangement of bodies inside an enclosure | none in KB | not excluded; the most machine-friendly ancient view |
| Stoics | pneuma, "the breath of life, congenital with us", a body [[29]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-stoics-soul-connate-pneuma-survives-until-conflagration) | warm pneuma grown with it | none in KB | not stated; "congenital" is the hurdle |
| Plotinus (Enn. IV.7) | the forming reason (λόγος) that makes a body; against anyone who says "an assemblage of atoms or impartibles produce soul by their union" [[7]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-plotinus-iv7-not-atoms) (Taylor) | a unifier that no assembly of parts produces; one perceiver of the whole [[30]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-plotinus-iv7-unity-of-perception) | none in KB | no: assembly cannot make the assembler |
| Proclus (Elements 186) | incorporeal, known by self-reversion: "every body is devoid of the power to turn toward itself" [[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-186-self-reversion-incorporeal) | to turn back on itself, which body is denied by definition | none in KB | no, by fiat about body |
| Asclepius (§23–24) | the divine life man "receives" and "gives" | a god drawn in, the statue made "from both natures" [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-hermetic) | yes: "man is the fashioner of the gods who dwell in temples" (*fictor deorum*) [[31]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-asclepius-man-fictor-deorum) (Scott) | yes, as housing |
| Egypt, via Budge (1898) | ka, "now generally rendered by "double"" [[32]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-budge-1898-ka-double-eidolon) | to be the image of a particular person | the ka "could even go and dwell in the statue of a man" [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-egypt-ka-statue) | yes, as housing; a 19th-c. reading |

[[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-golem) | a soul transferred from a pure maker | Rava's man: "He spoke with him, but he did not answer" [[33]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-bahir-rava-man-did-not-answer) | not yet; the fault is the maker's sin, not the clay |
