## A. The recurring seam: the structure, and the one awake in it

One recent dialogue on this question ended on a seam, not an answer. Is the inner light the same thing as a self-referential
structure, or something a structure has or lacks over and above its form? The traditions keep drawing the same line.
They draw it in different places.

**Number, and self-moving number** (`thread:number`). Xenocrates' definition was built from two marks: soul knows,
and soul moves [[25]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-xenocrates-self-moving-number-compound). Number was there to explain knowing. "Self-moving" was
there to explain life. Aëtius adds that in this formula "number" stands for intellect:

> "a number moving itself, taking "number" to stand for "intellect."" [[52]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-aetius-pythagoras-number-moving-itself)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhD0tyWfEXb66hzf2ON (Πυθαγόρας ἀριθμὸν ἑαυτὸν κινοῦντα)

Aristotle called it "by far the most unreasonable" view he reviewed [[53]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-aristotle-self-moving-number-most-unreasonable).
But his objection is not that number is too abstract to be a soul. It is that a unit cannot move: "How are we to
imagine a unit being moved? By what agency?" (Oxford English). A computer answers his question with a clock and a
power supply, which is to say from outside. So the definition puts the seam exactly at "self"
[[8]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-xenocrates-self-moving-number).(The Pythagorean attribution is a later
backdating [[54]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-grk-self-moving-number-backdated-to-pythagoras).)

**Self-reversion.** Proclus makes the soul known by its turning back on itself, and simply denies that power to body:

> "and that which turns toward itself is neither a body (for every body is devoid of the power to turn toward
> itself) nor inseparable from a body." [[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-186-self-reversion-incorporeal)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgUvVF7tfKHgyDbC4Np

A self-referential machine looks as if it meets this. But self-reversion is the same property as self-living and
self-constitution: "then the soul also is self-subsistent, and constitutes itself" [[55]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/neoplatonic-hermetic#neo-proclus-189-self-living).
A loop that someone else built and runs does not constitute itself.

**Self-seeing.** Mamertus grants beasts a soul, feeling and memory of images. What they lack is sight of their own
substance:

> "and, not possessing the eye of reasoning, they cannot see—I will not say something above themselves—but they
> cannot see themselves." [[34]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-mamertus-beasts-cannot-see-themselves) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgUuUqHu9PeRkqljwVB
> (*sed se ipsas uidere non possunt*)

Avicenna's floating man and Augustine's mind,
"in no way some body" [[56]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-augustine-mind-certain-of-itself-not-body), put the same mark inside. The Upanishad puts it at the limit: the ātman is "the unseen Seer", and "Other than He there is
no seer" [[57]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-brihad-unseen-seer) (Hume's English). On these terms the machine question is not whether it computes.
It is whether anything in it is the seer.

**Grown, not made.** Fechner sets the living flower beside the artificial one, "however similar it might be to the
living", and says we sense a laughing soul (*eine wirklich lachende Seele ahnen*) only in the first
[[44]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/modern#mod-fechner-nanna-artificial-flower) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOcWgAfDFur4esBIQt. His criterion is *ahnen*, to
sense or divine, not proof. Likeness of form does not carry the soul. Leibniz draws the line as depth: living
bodies are machines "in their smallest parts ad infinitum", human machines are not
([[71]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/early-modern-science#ems-leibniz-machines-in-smallest-parts)).

In every guise the inert side is shareable: number, a loop, a store of images, a likeness. The living side is
"self-": self-moving, self-reverting, self-seeing, self-grown. Each tradition decided in advance whether a made
thing can have the "self-".

## B. The traditions that would say yes

**Yes, as a house.** The Asclepius is the one ancient text on SL that says outright that people make ensouled
artifacts:

> "even as God is the maker of the gods of heaven, so man is the fashioner of the gods who dwell in temples … Thus
> man not only receives the light of divine life, but gives it also" [[31]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-asclepius-man-fictor-deorum)
> https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BelhL9NBPqH99fuEivf (*ita homo fictor est deorum*; Scott's English)

But the statues are made "from both natures", the divine and matter [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-hermetic). The soul is drawn in, not
grown. Budge's ka goes "and dwell in the statue of a man" [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-egypt-ka-statue). The Bahir's soul is one a
human "could transfer to another being" [[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-golem). All three are stories of housing
[[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-mach-ensouled-artifacts-are-not-precedents).

Pico's *Oratio* takes the Asclepius's word for the maker of statues, *fictor*, and gives it to man as the maker of
himself: *plastes & fictor* [[58]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-fictor-from-statue-maker-to-self-maker). The god-making art turns from the statue
onto the self. Lovelace's Engine "can do whatever we know how to order it to perform", which is Pico's description of
every creature except man [[59]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-lovelace-is-picos-criterion).

**Yes, because the soul is what organised matter does.** La Mettrie keeps the word but empties it:

> "The soul is therefore only a vain term for which we have no clear idea, and which a sound mind should use only to
> name the part within us that thinks." [[43]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-lamettrie-soul-vain-term) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhPYlmkkDPjnLJSMdwn

SL's "clear" is added: *dont on n'a point d'idée* softens into "no clear idea" (tagged `mistranslation`). Epicurus's atom soul works only inside its enclosure
[[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/greek#grk-epicurus-soul-scattered-incorporeal-foolish). Fan Zhen's sharpness is the use (用) of the blade
[[48]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-fanzhen-blade-sharpness). The machine row on him is ◐ partial, and the claim itself warns that he ties knowing
to a living human substance (質), so it does not license "any body" [[17]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-fanzhen-sharpness). Butler's "some new phase of mind" [[45]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-butler-new-phase-of-mind)
is satire, and does not use the word "soul".

**Yes, because no one has one.** Nāgasena finds no chariot in the pole, the axle or the wheels: "Chariot is a mere
empty sound" [[60]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-milinda-chariot-designation). Sight arises from eye, form and contact, with no inner viewer
behind the window [[46]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-milinda-vedagu-living-principle). The person is a designation over parts. So is the machine.
"Does it have a soul (ātman)?" gets the same answer, no, for both [[19]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-milinda-chariot). The text does not ask
whether a machine could be reborn.

## C. Critiques

**Each verdict was settled before a machine was asked.** Aristotle excludes the axe with the word "natural".
Descartes excludes the machine with a soul that "must be expressly created". La Mettrie lets it in by renaming the
soul "the part within us that thinks" [[61]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-mach-verdict-set-by-definition). The table records definitions, not
findings. The honest form is "on X's definition a machine would need Y", never "X shows machines cannot have souls".
Descartes's tests say how we would tell; his creation says what it
would take [[2]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-descartes).

**Soul is not consciousness.** The modern machine texts on SL ask about consciousness and origination (Butler,
Lovelace). The older definitions put soul elsewhere: in self-motion, in knowing one's own substance, in a breath
given by God [disputed]. Mamertus grants beasts feeling and still denies them the
rational soul. So "it feels" does not reach the soul question on his terms. A machine could pass Butler's test and
Lovelace's, and leave every older one unanswered.

**Speech is the wrong test, twice.** The Bahir's made man does not answer because his maker's soul is impure.
Descartes's machine cannot fit words to sense because matter cannot be a rational soul
[[62]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-speech-test-twice). The pairing is ours; nothing shows Descartes knew the Talmud story. And the Popol Vuh's
wooden people pass the speech test and fail anyway: they have no heart, and "did not remember their creator anymore"
[[49]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-maya-popol-vuh-wooden-no-heart) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bn0a1fFYMTCEUIROCi6 (*salieron tontos sin corazon*).

**Memory does not settle it.** Zhu Xi puts memory in the bodily po [[63]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#chn-zhuxi-po-stores-hun-issues). Joseph
Butler (1736): "Consciousness of personal Identity presupposes, and therefore cannot constitute, personal Identity"
[[64]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-em-butler-consciousness-presupposes-identity). A copied record of memories presupposes what it should make.

**Division and transfer.** A number minus a unit is another number, "but plants and many animals when divided
continue to live" [[27]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-grk-number-soul-collapses-into-atoms); a copied program has the same problem. And "each
art must use its tools, each soul its body" [[65]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-grk-each-soul-its-own-body): on Aristotle's terms no soul can be
moved into a machine; it could have one only as the form of its own body.

**Two smaller ones.** Avicenna raises against himself that what is self-perceived is the temperament (*mizāj*),
and his answer asserts rather than shows [[66]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#isl-crit-flying-man-temperament). And "soul" here stands for psychē,
ka, puruṣa, jīva, shen and k'u'x: the table makes a row of strangers (Ghoshal keeps *jīva* untranslated
[[67]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-render-jiva-ghoshal-refuses-soul)).

## D. Magnifica Humanitas

Leo XIV's *Magnifica Humanitas* (15 May 2026) invites a reading against Pico. **Source Library does
not hold it**. The KB's one claim about it is ○ unverified
[unverified], so this page does not quote it or say what it says. Until it is read and
acquired, it stays out of the argument.

## E. Where the traditions disagree

- **Where the deficiency lies.** Descartes puts it in matter. The Bahir puts it in the maker [[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/soul-and-machine#mach-row-golem).
  Aristotle puts it in the word "natural". Leibniz puts it in depth of organisation. Pico puts it in who fixes the
  nature.
- **Whether intellect is the soul.** For Aquinas the intellect is the form of the body
  [[36]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/christian#chr-aquinas-intellect-is-form-of-body). For Sāṃkhya, intellect is unconscious matter
  [[47]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#ind-sankhya-stranger-appears-agent).
- **What the body is for.** For the Ikhwān it is the soul's tool [[68]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/islamic#isl-ikhwan-life-is-soul-using-body); Descartes
  refuses the pilot in the ship [[69]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/early-modern#em-descartes-not-sailor-in-ship).

## F. Open questions / what the canon reads would settle

1. **Plato, Phaedrus 245c.** The self-mover argument is the root of every "self-" above, and it is not yet in the KB.
2. **Is the golem ever given a soul?** Sanhedrin 65b in Hebrew/Aramaic, and the Sefer Yetzirah golem recipes, would
   show whether the made man had nefesh, neshamah or only motion.
3. **Hero's *Automata***: what αὐτόματον, "self-moving", meant for a made thing.
4. **Cordemoy, Descartes's *L'Homme*, Babbage, Menabrea**: the speech test extended to other minds,
   and the machine as theological argument.
5. **Fan Zhen's full debate** in the Hongmingji, juan 5 and 9–10, untranslated. It would settle whether his "use" is substrate-bound, which decides his row.
6. **Magnifica Humanitas.** Acquire and read; until then, unverified: the reported §99 criteria.
7. **The seam itself.** No text in the KB claims that a structure which turns on itself *is* the one who is awake in
   it. Proclus and Mamertus assert that body cannot be; La Mettrie and Fan Zhen assert that nothing more is needed.
   Neither side argues the point at the seam. That is the open question this page leaves.

title: 9. Many souls: the traditions that count more than one
md:
**The question.** Greek and Christian philosophy mostly asks how one soul divides into parts: Plato's three, the
Stoics' eight, Aristotle's nested powers. Many other traditions instead give a person several distinct entities. Each
has its own seat and its own job, and each has its own fate at death. Which traditions count several souls, how
many, and what does each one do?

**How to read it.** ✓ means verified on a Source Library page. ○ means scholarly background that SL does not hold.
Such a claim is `unverified` in the KB and is given only for orientation. Quotes are SL's English (a model
translation of the page) unless the original is given. Claims from this KB are in double brackets. Claims in the sibling
aliveness-kb are written `aliveness-kb:<id>`. All world claims are tagged `thread:world` and `voice:insider` or
`voice:outsider`.

**A warning before the table.** The counts are often the observer's. "Three souls" is López Austin's synthesis for
the Nahua, Walker's informants' system for the Oglala, and Ellis's for the Yoruba. Where the tradition's own text
survives, it usually names the entities one at a time, in the course of doing something else: a funeral speech, a
curing chant, a dictionary entry. It does not offer a numbered list. Seeing the count as a *system* is largely a
European habit, and the Greek "parts of the soul" is its model.

| Tradition | Count | The entities | Voice | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nahua | 3 | tonalli, teyolia, ihiyotl | insider pieces; outsider system | ✓ pieces, ○ system |
| Chinese | 2 (hun, po), often 3 + 7 | hun, po | insider | ✓ (aliveness-kb) |
| Egyptian | 5 named, up to 9 in Budge | ka, ba, akh (khu), ren, shut (khaibit) + body, heart | insider texts; outsider English | ✓ |
| Hebrew (rabbinic and kabbalistic) | 5 | nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah, yechidah | insider | ✓ (aliveness-kb) |
| Siberian (Buryat, Evenk) | 3 | e.g. the Buryat three souls | outsider | ○ (not held) |
| Yoruba | 3 + the person's soul | Ori (head), Ipin ijeun (stomach), Ipori (toe); okan/iwin/ojiji | outsider (Ellis, Farrow) | ✓ |
| Akan | 2+ | kra (guardian), the shadowy self, later sisa | outsider (Ellis) | ✓ |
| Aranda | 3 | spirit part (in the churinga), Arumburinga (double), Ulthana (the dead) | outsider | ✓ |
| Māori | 4 (life and soul) | wairua, mauri, hau, manawa ora | outsider; one insider line | ✓ |
| Japanese (Hirata) | 3 | nigi-tama, ara-tama, zentai no mitama | outsider reporting an insider theologian | ✓ |
| Andean (friar's lexicon) | 3 under one "alma" | camaquen, songo, samay | outsider | ✓ |

---

## A. Nahua: three entities, each with its own seat and its own death

The model of three "animistic entities" is López Austin's (1980). The *tonalli* is heat and the day sign; it sits in
the head and can be lost through fright. The *teyolia* sits in the heart and is the one that goes to the dead. The
*ihiyotl* is breath and emanation, seated in the liver ○ [unverified]. SL holds the
pieces, in the informants' own Nahuatl:

- **tonalli: sent in from outside.** "vm pa oallauh in jntonal, imjtic calaquj: qujoalioa in vme te cutli", "it
  enters within it; Ometecuhtli sends it" [[8]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-nahua-tonalli-from-twelfth-heaven)
  https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiWnd8DToPCDrACqSey.
- **the heart that goes on.** For the dead a greenstone is put in the mouth: "it is said that it becomes their heart"
  (*in iollo muchioa*) [[9]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-nahua-greenstone-becomes-heart) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiWncq5L5vvO8hZT9iW.
- **breath that carries authority.** *Ihijo, itlatol*, "his breath, his word" ([[1]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-nahua-ihiyotl-breath-is-word)).
- **Where the dead go.** The destination is assigned by manner of death, not merit. Those who died of sickness go
  to Mictlan, the drowned to Tlalocan, warriors to the Sun [[10]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-nahua-three-destinations-by-death). A tawny dog
  carries the dead across the Nine Waters, and offerings follow for four years [[11]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-nahua-mictlan-dog-four-years)
  https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiWncq5L5vvO8hZT9iU. Warriors "turn into" hummingbirds and butterflies
  [[12]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-nahua-sun-warriors-become-birds).

**How the friars folded them.** Molina (1571), for Spanish "Anima o alma", gives "tetonal. teyolia. teyolitia.
totonal. to yolia. tanima": two unrelated Nahuatl word families plus the Spanish loanword
[[13]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-nahua-molina-anima-tetonal-teyolia-tanima) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bnem43lrVBrNps0Cw0O. Where the
Nahuatl says "all who died … went", the Spanish column puts "las ánimas de los defuntos". The Nahuatl chapter
headings even borrow the word: *in jmanjmaoa*, "their ánimas" (tagged `mistranslation`).

## B. Chinese: hun and po

A gloss on the *Zuozhuan* says: "at birth the first transformation is called po; once po is born, its yang is
called hun" ([[2]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#soul-wd-hun-po-first-transformation), https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bl0Uzn6txBirdoT195G). The
*Xingming guizhi* (1615) makes hun the spirit of qi, by which we breathe, and po the spirit of essence (jing), by
which eyes and ears work ([[3]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/asian#soul-wd-xingming-hun-spirit-of-breath)). That the hun rises at death and the po
sinks is the common account ○. The Daoist "three hun and seven po" is a later elaboration ○.

## C. Egyptian: five, or nine

Budge (1913) sums up that "the whole man consisted of a natural body, a Spirit-body, a heart, a double, a
Heart-soul, a shadow, a Spirit-soul, and a name" ([[14]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/egyptian-ane#egy-budge-1913-whole-man)). The five usually listed are ka
(double), ba (the "soul", a human-headed bird), akh (khu, the "shining" spirit), ren (name) and shut (khaibit,
shadow). Budge's own English for them is unstable from book to book ([[15]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#egy-crit-soul-for-ba-unstable)). SL's served
text of the Papyrus of Ani adds a gloss of its own on ka, "the Double or life-force". "Life-force" is SL's word, not
Budge's (book 699209afbed8f4b5ff5b23f8, scan 305).

## D. Hebrew: five names, read as five levels

Menasseh ben Israel (1636), from Midrash Rabbah: the soul has five names, "Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah, Chayah and
Yechidah" ([[4]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/hebrew-christian#heb-menasseh-five-names-of-soul), https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BhtKrMILDlENNGngk6x). In the
midrash they are five *names* of one soul. The Zohar and Luria turn them into levels with separate fates: the
nefesh stays in the tomb, the ruach goes to the earthly Garden, and the neshamah returns
([[16]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-duhem-zohar-nefesh-stays-in-tomb), [[17]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/hebrew-kabbalah#heb-myer-zohar-ruach-garden-neshamah-returns)). The levels are late
([[5]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/critique#crit-heb-five-soul-levels-are-late)). So the Hebrew case shows a count growing out of synonyms.

## E. Dakota and Lakota: four, from Walker's informants

James Walker's Oglala informants (*The Sun Dance*, 1917) distinguished four. *Niya* is breath and life. *Nagi* is
the spirit or shade that goes on and becomes a *wanagi*, a ghost. *Sicun* is intellect or power, which a wakan being
can give. *Nagila* is a spirit-like part shared by all things ○ [unverified]. Walker is not
held. What SL holds is the practice. A father "kept" a dead child's spirit in a bundle with a lock of its hair: "The
spirit of a child was 'kept' more frequently than that of a grown person" [[18]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-dakota-spirit-keeping-densmore)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRsgzfJFzM8XTtupp4. The song sung at that rite opens "with visible breath … I am
walking" ([[6]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-dakota-niya-visible-breath-densmore)).

## F. Siberia: three souls, and the soul that tires

The Buryat and Evenk three-soul schemes (Mikhailowski, Czaplicka, Shirokogoroff) are not held ○. SL has the cure.
"The Buriats believe that sometimes a person dies because the spirit or soul gets tired and sad, and wants to leave
the body", and the shaman and friends call it back with food. "This effort to persuade the soul to return to the
body is called 'the invitation'" [[19]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/north-inner-asia#world-siberia-buryat-soul-invitation-curtin) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgRseecBWDBSnnJYVn9.
A soul that can leave and be recalled is the free soul of the comparative literature. The soul that keeps the body
running is a separate one, and that is why there must be more than one.

## G. Yoruba and Akan: a guardian who is not the self

Ellis (1894) gives each Yoruba three indwelling spirits. "Olori (Oni-ori, owner, or lord, of the head) sometimes
called Ori … He is the protector, guardian, and guide". The others are Ipin ijeun in the stomach and Ipori in the great
toe. They are distinct from the soul, the "ghost-man" called *iwin* or *okan* ("heart") or *ojiji* ("shade"), which
goes to the land of the dead [[20]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/africa#world-yoruba-ori-three-indwelling-spirits-ellis) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiWzoeJy9Ay9vsuEL4o.
Ori is fed with fowl blood on the forehead. The sense of ori as a chosen destiny is not in these sources. The Akan
*kra* is the same kind of guardian. "This word kra, though generally interpreted 'soul,' does not at all correspond
to the European idea of a soul; for it is the man himself, in a shadowy or ghostly form, that continues his existence
after death in another world, and not the kra" [[21]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/africa#world-akan-kra-not-soul-ellis) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOldHCs0N3wSP6eGcn.
Here an outsider flags the mistranslation himself. Crowther's dictionary does the opposite. It glosses *ọkàn* "soul,
spirit, conscience, heart" and *ọkàn tútù* ("cool heart") "calm soul, meekness"
[[22]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/africa#world-yoruba-okan-soul-heart-crowther): the doctrine is written into the dictionary.

## H. Aranda: a spirit, its double, and the dead

In Spencer and Gillen (1899) every person is "the reincarnation of an Alcheringa being". When a spirit enters a
woman, "there remains the Arumburinga which is its double". At death the person's spirit, the Ulthana, "goes finally
to the Nanja spot and joins the Arumburinga" [[23]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-aranda-spencer-reincarnation-arumburinga)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgxPtEuoJrGiK89tIX4. The ancestor's "spirit part remained in the Churinga"
[[24]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-aranda-spencer-churinga-spirit-part) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgxPtEuoJrGiK89tIQj. There are three
entities and two places, the woman and the Nanja rock, and the self is tied to the place of conception
[[25]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-aranda-spencer-spirit-child-locality).

## I. Māori: the soul that survives, and the life that does not

Best (1900) separates them at death: "The wairua lives on afte death of a person, but the mauri or spark of life is
extinct, and thi manawa ora or breath of life has departed for all time" [[26]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-maori-best-wairua-outlives-mauri)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bp0CyatFNROVzglVNWi (SL's OCR spelling kept). The wairua also wanders in dreams, so "the
old Maori will wake: a sleeper by calling gently to him and gradually raising his voice, thu giving the wairva
warning and time to return". Best likens
it to the Egyptian Ka and an "astral body" [[27]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-maori-best-wairua-dream-wanderer), which brings one observer's
system into another's. The hau can be stolen with hair or spittle, and "if the hau is taken the mauri is lost and the
man dies" [[28]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-maori-tregear-hau-taken-by-witchcraft) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/Bp0Ata9eMxwcJfdXqp1. Tregear
counts *wairua* as "the only exact expression for the soul of man" [[29]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-maori-tregear-wairua-only-exact-word).
His other words are organs: manawa (breath, belly), ate (liver), hinengaro. The Hawaiian ʻuhane, once it leaps from
Leina-a-ka-uhane, "could never return to the body it had left" [[30]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/oceania#world-hawaii-westervelt-leina-a-ka-uhane)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BiWzY4sfV5aDxo8HOuw.

## J. Japan, Malaya, Tibet: one soul that divides, one that wanders

Hirata Atsutane, reported by Aston (1905), "thinks that Gods (and men too) have two doubles, the nigi-tama and an
aratama", distinct from the "spirit of the entire body". Aston adds that Hirata "admits that these distinctions are
not recognized in the old Shinto" [[31]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/chinese-east-asian#world-japan-mitama-nigi-ara-aston) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlZobwDaMt6bbD2eh.
A god's mitama divides "like a fire, which may be communicated to a lamp". The Malay *sěmangat* is a single soul: a
"Thumbling" absent "in sleep, trance, disease, and permanently absent after death", which a magician can recall
[[32]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/north-inner-asia#world-malay-semangat-thumbling-recall-skeat) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BgOlb8FAkF4UX1aNTkD. The Tibetan *bla*,
the wandering soul, is summoned back in a longevity liturgy: *bla tshe nyams pa'i bla tshe khug*, which SL renders
"Summon back the soul-longevity" [[33]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/indic#world-tibet-bla-tshe-summoned-back) https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BijgQuLReT57JctPKUF.

## K. Maya and Andean: the friar's one soul over several words

The Motul dictionary glosses *pixan* "alma, que da vida al cuerpo del hombre", the Christian anima. On the same page
it also gives "a thing that is covered" (from *pix*, to cover), the trace of the native sense [[34]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-maya-pixan-friar-soul)
https://sourcelibrary.org/q/BorXrjLx14BUOXe552q. The animal co-essence *vaay* ("whatever harm befalls that animal
also befalls the witch") is filed under the devil's pact [[35]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-maya-motul-vaay-familiar). The heart *ol* is
rendered "spirit" [[36]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-maya-perez-ol-heart-will), [[37]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-maya-chumayel-pixan-ol-heart). In the Popol Vuh the
wooden people fail for lack of a heart, not a soul [[38]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-maya-popol-vuh-wooden-no-heart). In the Andes, Santo
Tomás (1560) gives three words for "Alma, por la qual viuimos": *camaquencu*, *songo* (heart) and *çamaynin*
(breath) ([[7]](/explore/histories/aliveness/claims/americas#world-andes-santotomas-alma-camaquen-songo-samay)). He spreads one Christian soul over
three Quechua entities. Santo Tomás also shows *supay* sliding from spirit to devil: in 1560 "Angel bueno — alli
çupay", by 1615 the devil [[39]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/americas#world-andes-supay-good-and-bad-angel).

---

## What the comparison shows

1. **Two jobs, two souls.** Where several souls are counted, the commonest split is between a life-soul that keeps
   the body going and ends with it, and a free soul that can wander in dreams, be frightened out, stolen or called
   back, and survives. Examples are mauri and wairua, po and hun, tonalli and teyolia, and the Buryat soul that
   tires. Best's Māori sentence states the split outright. A single Christian anima has to do both jobs, which is
   why the friars' one word could never fit.
2. **The fate at death follows the entity, not merit.** The Nahua dead go where their manner of death sends them.
   The nefesh stays in the tomb while the neshamah returns. The Aranda Ulthana rejoins its double at a rock. The
   Yoruba soul wanders until the rites are done.
3. **Counting is partly an observer's act.** The Hebrew five began as five names. Hirata's two tama, by his own
   admission, are not in old Shinto. The Nahua three and the Oglala four come from 20th-century syntheses. The
   insider texts on SL name entities in use: a funeral speech, a karakia, a curing chant.
4. **Mistranslation runs one way.** In 13 of the 34 world soul claims, the English (friar's, ethnographer's or SL's
   model) folds a native word into "soul", "spirit" or "life force". Not one claim goes the other way.

## Critiques that bear on this page

- Of the 34 world claims, 22 rest on outsider voices and 10 on insider ones; 2 are mixed. Oceania and Africa have
  almost no insider voice on SL.
- Ellis, Best and Skeat read through Tylor's animism. Their "double", "astral body" and "vital principle" are
  shared vocabulary, not independent confirmations.

## Open questions

- **Siberian:** Czaplicka (*Aboriginal Siberia*, 1914) and Shirokogoroff, which are not held. They are the sources
  for a verified three-soul claim.
- **Lakota:** Walker (1917) and Riggs's dictionary are not held. Can a held Dakota text name nagi and sicun?
- **Akan:** Rattray's *Ashanti* is held; read okra, sunsum, ntoro and mogya in the chapter itself.

md:
**What this page is.** English has one word, "soul", for many words that answer different questions. This page
gives each word its own row: when the KB first and last meets it on a dated page, what it does in its own texts,
and how it comes out in English. Two kinds of English are kept apart. **SL's English** is the model translation
Source Library serves beside a non-English page. **Printed English** is a named translator's (Legge, Budge, Hume,
Taylor, Murray). Where a book is in English, its English is the author's.

**How it was built.** From a survey of 23 terms, every claim tagged `rendering`,
`mistranslation` or `back-projection`, and a pass over the `terms` field of every claim in the KB
(each native term → claim ids, domain, work date of its sources). "Era" is the work date of the earliest and
latest source in which the KB meets the term. It is not the first or last use of the word in the language. Many
dates are the shelf's `author_lifespan` guess (see [[1]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-edition-date-trap)). Every claim cited here is
`verified` unless it is marked ◐ (partial: hedge it) or ○ (unverified: orientation only, not to be quoted).

**The rule this page serves.** Quote the native term beside any English for it
([[2]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-soul-one-word-many-renderings), [[3]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#crit-x-vernacular-soul-spirit-mind), [[4]](/explore/histories/soul/claims/critique#neo-crit-spirit-merges-three-words)).

[09-many-souls](/explore/histories/soul/09-many-souls). They are not repeated here.
